Oil surges, stocks sink as US reportedly eyes new Iran strikes
item.description:
Oil prices soared more than five per cent Thursday following reports that the United States could launch fresh attacks on Iran before next month's midterm elections, risking further supply disruptions.

Brent North Sea crude, the international benchmark, rallied to $105.48 a barrel before paring gains. The main US contract, West Texas Intermediate, reached as high as $92.84 per barrel.

The Atlantic magazine reported that the White House had asked the Pentagon to draw up options for hitting sites in Iran ahead of the congressional midterms on 3 November.

With Donald Trump's Republicans in danger of losing both houses of Congress, an escalation in the US-Iran conflict could put even more pressure on the president, with Americans already battling record-high diesel prices.

But the suggestion is that renewed US attacks could strengthen Trump's position in seeking to bring Tehran to the negotiating table to end the war.

"The planning (for possible fresh strikes) should be seen in the context of efforts to pressure Iran, bring energy prices down, and demonstrate progress in the conflict ahead of the election," said Arne Lohmann Rasmussen, chief analyst at the energy consulting firm Global Risk Management.

Meanwhile Yemen's Houthis targeted Riyadh airport with missiles on Thursday and warned staff at oil facilities in Saudi Arabia to leave to avoid being targeted as hostilities escalate.

The surge in oil prices weighed on stock markets, with Wall Street's main indices moving lower at the opening bell.

In Europe, both Frankfurt and Paris were lower but London added 0.2 per cent as the higher oil price benefited energy majors. Shares in BP rose 3.3 per cent and Shell 3.2 per cent in afternoon trading.

Asia's leading stock markets tracked losses Wednesday on Wall Street, where technology firms pulled back from recent gains.

Shares in Samsung slid as the South Korean titan forecast a huge increase in quarterly profit that nonetheless failed to meet market expectations.

On Wall Street, shares in SpaceX slid 0.9 per cent as trading got under way in New York, following a Financial Times report that Elon Musk's firm is aiming to raise $40 billion in bank loans and debt to further its purchases of AI chips from Nvidia.

The massive fundraising, coming just four months after SpaceX raised $86 billion in the world's biggest IPO, underscored the voracious demand among tech firms for chips to roll out their ambitions surrounding artificial intelligence.

On currency markets, the euro remains near lows last seen in June 2025 on worries about France's high debt levels, which have spooked bond investors.

item.description:
In the first half of this year (January-June), Bangladeshi apparel exports to the US market decreased by almost six per cent.

By the end of July, it increased to six and a half per cent.

However, in August, the rate of decline decreased, with apparel exports decreasing by 4.43 per cent.

During the same period, apparel exports from China and India to the United States declined by more than 29 and 26 per cent, respectively.

Even though the decline in apparel exports to the US market slightly decreased, Bangladesh lost its second position to China.

At the end of July, Bangladesh was the second largest apparel exporting country after Vietnam, followed by China.

However, by the end of August, China had taken over Bangladesh's second position.

Bangladesh is now in third place, with a difference of 240 million USD in apparel exports between Bangladesh and China.

This picture emerged from updated data published by the US Office of Textiles and Apparel (OTEXA). The data shows that in the first eight months of this year (January-August), US apparel imports decreased by 7.42 per cent.

During this time, US traders imported apparel worth 49 billion or 4,900 crore USD.

Analysing OTEXA’s data reveals that in the first eight months of this year, the volume of US apparel imports decreased by 8.98 per cent.

Consequently, the average price per square meter of apparel increased by 1.71 per cent, although the average price of apparel exported from Bangladesh decreased.

During the January-August period of this year, Bangladesh exported apparel worth 5.39 billion USD to the US market, which is 4.43 per cent less compared to the same period last year. The decline in Bangladesh's exports is almost 3 percentage points more than the overall decrease in US apparel imports.

Meanwhile, in terms of volume, Bangladesh exported 1.76 billion square meters of apparel in the first eight months of this year, which is almost 3 per cent less than the same period last year. During this time, the average price per square meter of apparel exported from Bangladesh was 3.07 USD, which is a decrease of 1.73 per cent compared to the same period last year.

Among the countries supplying apparel to the US market, China experienced the largest decline. In the first eight months of this year, China exported apparel worth 5.63 billion USD, which is a decrease of 29.39 per cent compared to the same period last year.

During the same period, India's exports decreased by 26.44 per cent, and Pakistan’s apparel exports decreased by 3.83 per cent. On the other hand, apparel exports from Indonesia and Cambodia increased by 2.58 per cent and 6.91 per cent, respectively.

Vietnam is the top apparel-exporting country to the US market. In the first eight months of this year, it exported apparel worth 10.98 billion USD, a decrease of 0. 76 per cent compared to the same period last year. The average price per square meter of apparel exported from Vietnam was 3. 54 USD, a 0.58 per cent decrease compared to last year.

Among the top 10 exporting countries, the price of Chinese apparel decreased by 9. 93 per cent. In the first eight months of this year, the average price per square meter of apparel exported from China was 1.47 USD, which is half the price of apparel from Bangladesh.

The price of apparel exported from Pakistan to the US from Bangladesh is also low, with the price per square meter equivalent apparel being 2.78 USD.

item.title: Australia provides Tk 1.55b to support Rohingyas, host communities in Bangladesh
item.description:
Australia has signed an AUD18 million (about Tk 1.55 billion) agreement with BRAC to support Rohingya refugees and host communities in Bangladesh.

Australian High Commissioner Susan Ryle and BRAC Executive Director Asif Saleh signed the agreement. The announcement was made in the presence of Disaster Management and Relief Minister Asadul Habib Dulu.

The funding will provide flexible, multi-year support for essential services for Rohingya refugees and host communities in Cox’s Bazar and Bhasan Char, according to a press release issued by the Australian High Commission.

Under the agreement, BRAC will provide support in areas including healthcare, water and sanitation, education, disaster risk management, skills development and protection services in the refugee camps and surrounding host communities.

The programme will also support local organisations through BRAC’s localisation fund. The fund is intended to strengthen the capacity of national partners, support cost-effective delivery of services at scale and expand coverage in underserved camps, according to the release.

The new agreement is part of Australia’s AUD370 million (about Tk 31.6 billion) humanitarian package for 2026–2028. The package will support Rohingya refugees and host communities in Bangladesh as well as people affected by the crisis in Myanmar.

Since 2017, Australia has committed AUD1.26 billion (about Tk 107.7 billion) in humanitarian assistance in response to the regional crisis, the release said.

Australia remains committed to supporting the Bangladesh government in providing humanitarian assistance to displaced Rohingyas and their host communities, it said.

The Australian government said continued access to essential support for the Rohingya was critical until conditions are in place for their voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable return to Myanmar.

item.title: CPA, DP World sign deal to boost Chittagong port capacity
item.description:
Chittagong Port Authority (CPA) and global port operator DP World on Thursday signed a 15-year concession agreement for the operation and modernisation of the New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT), marking a major step towards improving the efficiency and capacity of Bangladesh’s principal maritime gateway.

CPA Chairman Rear Admiral SM Moniruzzaman signed the agreement on behalf of the Chittagong Port Authority, while DP World Chairman Essa Kazim signed on behalf of the international terminal operator at a ceremony held at Invest Bangladesh auditorium here.

Shipping Minister Sheikh Rabiul Alam, State Minister for Shipping Md Rajib Ahsan, UAE Ambassador to Bangladesh Abdulla Ali Al Hamoudi and Invest Bangladesh Chairman Ashik Chowdhury, among others, attended the signing ceremony.

Under the concession, DP World will operate and manage NCT for an initial period of 15 years, while ownership of the terminal’s land, core infrastructure and assets will remain with CPA and, ultimately, the government of Bangladesh.

The agreement provides an upfront payment of around Tk 6 billion, with 25 per cent payable upon signing and the remaining 75 per cent before commencement of operations.

DP World will also invest more than Tk 10 billion during the first 10 years to modernise the terminal through new equipment, technology and operational improvements.

In addition, CPA will receive a share of terminal revenue or royalty, ranging from around 40 per cent to 67 per cent per TEU depending on average terminal revenue, along with a fixed annual fee of approximately Tk 100 million.

NCT handover to DP World sparks protest in capital, police baton-charge

The agreement includes a minimum annual volume guarantee of 1.23 million TEUs, with provision for adjustment to 1 million TEUs once a new terminal becomes operational.

Speaking at the ceremony, Shipping Minister Sheikh Rabiul Alam said the government’s objective was to rapidly increase the capacity and efficiency of existing strategic assets.

“Modern equipment, digital systems, international operating standards and global logistics connections will make NCT more competitive,” he said.

He said the government’s wider policy was to engage multiple international operators across terminals to improve service quality and reliability and strengthen supply-chain resilience.

DP World Chairman Essa Kazim said Bangladesh was becoming an increasingly important trading and manufacturing economy and DP World was committed to supporting its continued development.

“Through this partnership, DP World will connect the New Mooring Container Terminal to our global network of ports, logistics infrastructure and supply chain services, helping create more seamless links between Bangladesh and international markets,” he said.

He said the company would combine its operational expertise, technology and end-to-end logistics capabilities to support trade, attract investment and create new opportunities for businesses across Bangladesh.

CPA Chairman Rear Admiral Md Moniruzzaman said the partnership reflected Bangladesh’s commitment to strengthening its maritime and trade infrastructure through the public-private partnership framework.

He said the agreement would enhance operational performance, ease logistics constraints and strengthen connectivity with international markets.

item.title: Bangladesh signs 15-year deal with DP World to operate NCT
item.description:
Bangladesh on Thursday signed a 15-year agreement with UAE-based DP World to operate and maintain Chittagong Port’s New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) and its overflow container yard.
The agreement was signed at 3:40pm.
Chittagong Port Authority Chairman Rear Admiral SM Moniruzzaman and DP World Chairman and CEO Sultan Ahmed bin Sulayem signed the agreement.
The process of appointing an international operator for NCT began in 2019.
In March 2023, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs gave in-principle approval to appoint an international private operator under a public-private partnership framework.
The interim government later revived the initiative and selected DP World. However, the process stalled amid opposition and a workers’ strike earlier this year. The current government subsequently resumed negotiations.
Built in 2007 at a cost of around Tk2,000 crore, NCT has five jetties. Fourteen of Chittagong Port’s 18 quayside gantry cranes are located at the terminal.
More than 40% of the port’s container handling is carried out through NCT.
The project initially received in-principle approval from the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs in March 2023. The latest approval relates to the draft concession agreement governing the terminal’s operation and maintenance for 15 years.
Meanwhile, the Chittagong Port Protection Committee has been holding various programmes demanding the cancellation of the process to lease the terminal to a foreign company.

item.title: Salahuddin: Govt to set up two army camps in hills near Rohingya camps
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said the government has decided to set up two new army camps in the hilly areas adjacent to the Rohingya camps to prevent crimes including abductions.
He made the remarks to journalists at the Secretariat around 3pm on Thursday, after a meeting titled “Meeting for the Overall Improvement of Law and Order in Jungle Salimpur, Chittagong.”
The home minister said the two camps would be established in the hills of Rangikhali and Noakhalipara in Teknaf under the leadership of the 10th Infantry Division of Ramu.
He said abductions and other incidents occur regularly in the two hilly areas. To prevent these crimes, a decision has been made to set up two camps in the area under the leadership of the 10th Infantry Division.
The meeting expressed the view that once the two camps are established, such crimes in the area will be eliminated.
He said joint operations are conducted to address the law and order situation inside and outside the Rohingya camps. These operations are being carried out against various crimes, including drugs, weapons and human trafficking.
A deputy inspector general (DIG) of the Armed Police Battalion leads the operations, with other law enforcement agencies also involved.
The home minister also mentioned a decision to rebuild the fencing, or barbed-wire barrier, to strengthen security at the Rohingya camps.
In addition, solar-powered lighting will be arranged outside the camps. Closed-circuit television (CCTV) cameras will be installed at fixed intervals, and control towers and watchtowers will be built.
He further said that in the event of a war or any emergency, the army will lead the response. A Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) has been set for this purpose.

item.title: Bangladesh’s GDP growth rebounds to 4.60% in FY26 final quarter
item.description:
Bangladesh’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth surged to 4.60% in the final quarter (April–June) of FY26, up significantly from 2.05% recorded during the same period in the previous fiscal year.
According to the latest quarterly estimates released by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), this economic acceleration was primarily fueled by a strong turnaround in the industrial sector.
At current prices, the quarterly GDP size reached Tk1,611,700 crore, compared to Tk1,438,500 crore in the fourth quarter of FY25.
On an annual consolidated basis across all four quarters, overall GDP growth for FY26 stood at 3.68%.
A sector-wise analysis on a point-to-point basis at constant prices reveals a powerful rebound in the industrial sector, which expanded by 6.52% in the fourth quarter compared to just 0.92% in the corresponding period of FY25.
The manufacturing sub-sector served as the chief growth driver within industry, delivering an 8.66% expansion.
The services sector also saw improved performance, growing by 4.28% compared to 2.26% in the same quarter of the prior year.
Conversely, the agriculture sector slowed down, recording a growth rate of 1.73% in the April–June 2026 quarter, down from 3.19% in the fourth quarter of FY25.
BBS data shows that GDP growth rates for the first three quarters of FY26 were estimated at 4.96%, 3.03%, and 2.22% respectively, compared to 3.91%, 3.53%, and 4.53% during the same quarters of FY25.
The statistical bureau has been regularly compiling and publishing quarterly GDP estimates using the production method since the first quarter of FY24 to align with international standards and assist in tracking short-term economic trends, policy formulation, and national planning.

item.title: Myanmar leader says will take back migrants from Malaysia ‘as soon as possible’
item.description:
Myanmar will accept more Burmese migrants held in Malaysia “as soon as possible,” the war-torn nation’s leader said Thursday despite human rights concerns over the opaque repatriation scheme.
Min Aung Hlaing made the pledge on a visit to his counterpart in Malaysia, as he works to bring his country back into the international fold after staging a 2021 coup.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim invited Min Aung Hlaing, now installed as civilian president, for a two-day visit to discuss the return of thousands of migrants to his country.
Malaysia has historically offered safe haven to those exiled from Myanmar, hosting 190,000 refugees or asylum seekers from the nation -- mostly Rohingya -- according to the United Nations (UN).
But Anwar is making a repatriation push amidst an uptick of anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia, defying concerns from the UN that his scheme cannot guarantee their safe homecomings to Myanmar.
The country has been wracked by war since Min Aung Hlaing’s putsch, and there are fears the persecuted Rohingya may return to a country where they suffer violent persecution many deem genocide.
“We will take those verified nationals back as soon as possible,” Min Aung Hlaing said at a joint news conference with Anwar, in Putrajaya, the administrative capital.
Min Aung Hlaing has been a pariah in many capitals abroad since his putsch unleashed a civil war, but Anwar invited him for talks about returning Myanmar migrants.
Nearly 1,500 migrants arrived in back in Myanmar on Sunday after a five-day navy vessel voyage from Malaysia, where they were being held in detention centers before being shipped out.
Anwar in July announced that Myanmar agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya members, but the Malaysian government later said those sent back would be of “various ethnicities,” not only Rohingya.
Myanmar last month pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after criticism from the UN and rights groups.
Min Aung Hlaing’s two-day trip also comes as he makes a push for diplomatic recognition after being installed in April as civilian president, following elections branded a charade by democracy watchdogs.
Leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) said in July they were seeking “gradual” engagement with Myanmar.
The 11-nation organization has frozen Myanmar out of high-level summits since the coup, presenting a united front to pressure its leaders into engaging in its conflict resolution plan.
But analysts say the consensus is now fraying.
Malaysia marks the fifth Asean nation to host Min Aung Hlaing since he transitioned to ruling the country as nominally civilian president.
A five-point peace plan adopted by Asean’s leaders in April 2021, which among other things call for an immediate cessation of violence in Myanmar, has shown very little signs of progress.
This was highlighted by a Myanmar military air strike late last month on a market in western Myanmar killing some 50 people -- one of the deadliest recent bombings of the civil war.
Said Anwar on Thursday: “We and (for) our part in Malaysia will do whatever is possible to make sure that we enhance this collaboration.”
The aim ultimately was to “take Myanmar as part of our community of nations without prejudice, and particularly in the context of Asean.”

item.title: Russian strike on buses kills 30 in frontline Ukrainian city
item.description:
Ukraine on Thursday accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilians after 30 people were killed when two buses were blown up in the frontline city of Kramatorsk, in one of the deadliest single attacks for weeks.
Photos posted by local authorities showed the burnt-out metal shell of the vehicles, with the blurred-out images of bodies and debris strewn across the road.
Police said the buses were hit with a glide bomb.
The strikes come just a day after five children were among 22 killed when a Russian missile struck a five-story apartment block in Pryluky, in the northern Chernigiv region.
“The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” Donetsk Governor Vadym Filashkin said, accusing Moscow of flouting “every conceivable rule of warfare and norm of international humanitarian law.”
Kramatorsk City Council called it “yet another horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population.”
“Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets,” it added.
There has been mounting concern about the increase in civilian casualties in the conflict, as both sides step up long-range attacks beyond their borders.
Since Russia first invaded in 2022, Ukraine has accused its forces of deliberately attacking and killing civilians.
The United Nations has verified more than 17,000 civilian deaths throughout the war, but says the real number is considerably higher.
Last week, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin had sanctioned massive attacks on civilian areas.
The Kremlin has denied the claim.
Ukraine’s capital, Kyiv, has come under increasing attack, including on Wednesday when Russia launched a barrage of powerful ballistic and cruise missiles, and fast-moving, jet-powered drones.
The city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said two people were found dead on Thursday after a fire at a four-story building that was hit by a drone in the densely populated Solomyansky district.
Klitschko has said the attacks, which have hit key transport bridges in the city, as well as the rail network and energy grid, were “tearing Kyiv apart.”
For the first few years of the war, Kyiv had been relatively spared from the devastation wrought on the frontline but should now be on a war footing, he argued.
Kramatorsk, which was home to some 150,000 people before the war, is one of the key cities that Russia has not yet captured in the eastern Donetsk region, which Moscow claims as its own.
It has been a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military for much of the war and is part of the so-called “fortress belt” which troops are fighting to keep hold of.
Russian forces have edged close to the city’s eastern fringes, which has prompted calls for the civilians who remain to relocate to safer regions of Ukraine.
Filashkin said Thursday’s strike, which happened at 10am (0700 GMT), represented a “sharp deterioration” in security and ordered the suspension of public transport in Kramatorsk and neighboring Sloviansk.
“Under these circumstances, we cannot risk the lives of passengers and drivers,” he said. “The safety of the residents of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk is now our top priority.”
Ukraine last month launched a counter-offensive against Russian troops around Lyman -- to the north of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk -- claiming some success in regaining pockets of territory.

US opens direct talks with Myanmar's generals, reversing years of isolation
item.description:
MALAYSIA-MYANMAR/

The Trump administration has begun direct talks with Myanmar’s military-installed government, according to US officials and others familiar with the outreach, in a sharp reversal of Washington's efforts to isolate the country’s generals after the 2021 coup.

The US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research, Michael Vance, played a leading role in the outreach, which has focused on shutting down scam centers that target Americans but could lead to broader engagement, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits, according to seven current and former officials and others familiar with the policy shift.

Vance joined talks with coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing in the capital Naypyitaw on September 15-16. The meeting was aimed at securing the release of American businessman Adam Castillo but also provided an opening for further engagement, four of the people said.

Last month’s meeting — the highest‑level contact since the coup — underscores a broader Trump‑administration foreign policy tilt away from democracy promotion toward transactional engagement.

The presence of Vance, who was confirmed as the State Department’s top intelligence official in August, and his ongoing role in US policy toward Myanmar have not been previously reported.

Military leader remains under US sanctions

Min Aung Hlaing, the former military chief, remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of hundreds of thousands of Rohingya Muslims that Washington declared a genocide. Less than two weeks after Vance’s visit, Myanmar’s military conducted an airstrike on a crowded marketplace in Rakhine state, killing over 50 people and injuring scores more, according to United Nations human rights officials.

The State Department said it engages with all groups in Myanmar on issues affecting US interests and raises the need to cease violence and release political prisoners.

“You don't solve problems by ignoring them. You solve problems by addressing them,” spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a statement.

A spokesperson for the military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment. Min Aung Hlaing, who has cited electoral fraud to justify the coup and labeled his opponents as terrorists, is seeking international legitimacy for his nominally civilian government.

Current and former officials say Vance has met players from all sides of Myanmar’s complex conflict and helped shape the Trump administration’s policy toward the country.

Intelligence chiefs — such as Vance — do not typically steer policy because of concerns about compromising analytic independence.

“If you let policy dictate to intelligence, you can't be sure you're getting a real honest assessment of the facts,” said Richard Betts, an adjunct senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations who has consulted for US intelligence agencies.

Pigott declined to address Vance’s role but said the administration “operates as a team with the president as the lead.”

A detained American, and an opening

Castillo, a former head of the American Chamber of Commerce in Myanmar, was detained at Yangon airport on 11 June by Myanmar authorities on what his supporters have described as trumped-up charges. The US government has not commented on whether Castillo was wrongfully detained.

People familiar with the matter said White House, National Security Council and State Department officials held back-channel negotiations with Myanmar officials to secure his release. One person said Myanmar asked only "to have an official engagement at the right level with the US government" in return.

Castillo declined to comment beyond crediting President Donald Trump for his release.

The meeting builds on a June meeting between US and Myanmar officials in Tokyo also involving Vance, four people said. One of the people said officials from the Treasury Department, which oversees sanctions, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Pentagon took part.

It was unclear who represented Myanmar at the talks.

Vance, who became involved in Myanmar policy while advising Vice President JD Vance on Asian affairs, has also met in person and virtually with the democratic opposition and ethnic armed groups fighting the military, five of the people said.

A major focus of the US push is getting Myanmar's help shuttering scam hubsoperating on its territory that run romance and other frauds, which have scammed Americans out of billions of dollars. Two people familiar with the matter said the FBI has had direct contact with Myanmar’s authorities on cyber scams.

Researchers say many scams are run from areas under militia control, with some proceeds flowing to the military, raising doubts about whether Myanmar’s leaders are serious about enforcement.

US officials also discussed access to Myanmar’s massive deposits of heavy rare earths that are used in electric vehicles and wind turbines. US officials acknowledge obstacles: the deposits mainly lie in territory held by ethnic armies fighting Myanmar’s military government, and China, currently the main importer, could see any US role as a challenge.

Still, with Washington seeking to diversify supply chains away from China, Myanmar's deposits remain a recurring topic in conversations, the people said.

From sanctions to engagement

After the 2021 coup, President Joe Biden's administration froze Myanmar's assets at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and imposed sanctions on senior officers and military‑linked businesses.

In 2022, Congress authorized non-lethal support for the opposition, funding early-warning systems for airstrikes and incentives for officers to defect.

Most of those programs were cut during Trump’s foreign-aid overhaul last year, according to four current and former officials and State Department correspondence with Congress reviewed by Reuters.

The State Department said its engagement with the military government does not diminish its relationships with other groups. The US continues to provide assistance to areas outside military control, it said, without detailing that aid.

Representative Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said the shift was “contrary to both our values and our interests.”

“By engaging Min Aung Hlaing while failing to implement congressionally mandated sanctions and deploy appropriated democracy funding, Secretary (Marco) Rubio is ceding U.S. leadership and providing this murderous regime greater international legitimacy,” Meeks said in a statement to Reuters.

Myanmar's government, installed after elections criticized by rights groups as a sham, has hired lobbyists to press its case in Washington.

In April, Roger Stone, a longtime Trump adviser, began consulting for DCI Group on behalf of Myanmar's Ministry of Information, according to Foreign Agents Registration Act filings. Stone was convicted in 2019 of obstructing a congressional investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. Trump later pardoned him.

A newsletter distributed by DCI warned in June that Washington risked being shut out of access to critical minerals if it did not engage with Myanmar.

item.title: Pentagon prepares for fresh Iran strikes ahead of US midterms
item.description:
The Pentagon has instructed US Central Command to complete preparations for a possible resumption of major military operations against Iran, raising the prospect of another wave of US-Israeli strikes as President Donald Trump weighs his options ahead of crucial elections in both countries.
The directive was issued several days ago, American news website Axios reported exclusively on Wednesday, citing US officials familiar with the preparations.
Although no date has been set and Trump has not made a final decision, US and Israeli officials told Axios that renewed attacks could take place before the November 3 US midterm elections, potentially even before Israel’s October 27 elections.
Any renewed offensive could involve extensive bombing of Iranian energy infrastructure, military installations and nuclear facilities, according to the report.
The preparations mark a potentially significant escalation in the conflict, which began with US and Israeli strikes on February 28 and has since disrupted regional security and global energy markets.
A fresh military campaign could also drive up oil prices, particularly given the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz, and carry political consequences for both Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
However, military preparations do not necessarily mean an attack is imminent.
“The Department’s job is to develop and present military options to the President,” a Pentagon official told Axios.
A White House official said Trump retained all military options and would act according to US interests.
The official claimed Washington was in a strong position because of its control over the Strait of Hormuz and the pressure on Iran’s economy.
The Pentagon directive follows a meeting of Trump’s senior national security team at Camp David on Friday, where the possibility of renewed major combat operations against Iran was discussed, according to Axios.
The meeting included Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and other senior officials.
Rubio subsequently described the gathering as part of long-term foreign policy planning.
The military preparations come as US-Iran negotiations remain deadlocked, particularly over Tehran’s nuclear program.
Qatari mediators are awaiting Iran’s response to a US counterproposal seeking nuclear concessions, Axios reported.
Iran continues to insist on its right to enrich uranium, while Washington is demanding substantial restrictions on its nuclear activities.
The diplomatic impasse has increased concerns that military action could again become Washington’s preferred option.
The Atlantic also reported Wednesday that Trump was considering strikes before the midterm elections, citing administration officials.
Trump spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Wednesday, their second conversation in recent days following a lengthy period of limited contact.
According to Axios, the conversation followed a meeting Netanyahu held with his national security team about Iran.
Netanyahu also spoke with Rubio on Monday.
US and Israeli officials believe any renewed large-scale offensive would likely involve coordinated military operations by both countries.
Israeli officials also warned that Iran could respond with extensive ballistic missile attacks against Israel.
One Israeli official told Axios that discussions about resuming major combat operations had intensified, although an attack before the elections was considered less likely than one afterward.
The possibility of renewed fighting comes amid mounting political pressure on both governments.
For Trump, another military campaign could complicate the November 3 midterm elections, particularly if oil prices rise sharply or US forces suffer casualties.
For Netanyahu, an escalation before Israel’s October 27 elections could reshape the final stages of the campaign, although its political consequences remain uncertain.
Trump has repeatedly signalled in recent weeks that he could authorize another major offensive if negotiations fail.
In a September 17 interview with Axios, he said he was approaching a major decision on Iran.
During his September 22 address to the United Nations General Assembly, he again warned Tehran of severe consequences if it refused Washington’s nuclear demands.
In an interview with Time published on October 1, Trump acknowledged that expanded military operations after the US midterms remained possible.
He has also suggested that the conflict could end before or shortly after the elections, while accusing Iran of delaying negotiations in anticipation of a more favorable political environment.
The war, which began with US and Israeli attacks on February 28, has already caused major disruption to regional energy markets and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Renewed bombing of Iranian energy facilities could deepen those disruptions, while Iranian retaliation could threaten Israel, US military installations and Gulf energy infrastructure.
For now, the distinction remains critical: The Pentagon has been ordered to prepare for major combat operations, but Trump has not authorized a new offensive.
The latest directive nevertheless places US forces closer to operational readiness as diplomatic efforts struggle to produce an agreement.

item.title: Rooppur Unit 1 gets approval to begin nuclear reaction
item.description:
Bangladesh has received approval to begin a nuclear reaction at the first unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant, bringing the country closer to generating nuclear power for the first time.
If the process proceeds as planned, the unit could supply 300MW of electricity to the national grid in December.
According to media reports, the process was initially scheduled to begin in September but was delayed after a fault was detected during safety-valve testing.
Two high-pressure tests were conducted last week, and the results were submitted to the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA).
BAERA approved the results on Thursday, clearing the way for the next stage of work.
BAERA Chairman Mahmud Hasan told the media that each stage of the Rooppur plant is approved only after safety is verified.
“After verification by local and international experts, the licence for the next stage was issued today (Thursday),” he said. “Work on this stage will begin on Friday. It should not take long to complete, and the nuclear reaction is expected to begin within two to three days.”
Meanwhile, two safety-valve tests were completed last week to check whether the control valves were functioning properly. The tests were conducted according to prescribed procedures, while fire and radiation safety measures were also checked beforehand.
The process of generating heat inside the reactor vessel could begin by the end of this month, according to media reports.
The Rooppur plant in Pabna consists of two Russian-built VVER-1200 reactors, each designed to generate 1,200MW. Together, the two units are expected to provide 2,400MW of electricity.
Bangladesh’s plans to build a nuclear power plant date back decades. The project gained momentum after Bangladesh signed an agreement with Russia in 2011 to cooperate on the plant, leading to the construction of the two VVER-1200 reactors at the Pabna site.

item.title: Thirty five power plants shut, load shedding hits 2,500MW
item.description:
As many as 35 power plants remain shut across the country, pushing load shedding to 2,500MW amid a worsening fuel shortage.
The simultaneous shutdown of so many plants has raised concerns. Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) officials said fuel shortages, particularly inadequate gas supplies, are the main reason behind the closures.
Gas-fired plants cannot generate electricity at full capacity due to insufficient gas supplies. Liquid-fuelled plants face a similar problem, as operating them requires substantial financial resources.
A Power Division official said electricity generated from furnace oil currently costs around Tk25 per unit, compared with Tk13-14 from coal and about Tk7 from gas.
“Gas remains the cheapest source of electricity, but we cannot ensure adequate supplies despite the demand,” the official said.
He said Bangladesh currently receives around 1,600 million cubic feet of gas per day from domestic sources and another 1,000mmcfd from imported LNG. Supplies from either source cannot be increased overnight, as no significant new gas reserves have been found onshore and the country lacks sufficient infrastructure to increase LNG imports.
On October 7, gas-fired power plants had a combined demand of 2,524mmcfd, against a supply of only 895mmcfd.
Officials said increasing gas supplies to power plants could worsen shortages in the industrial sector and disrupt exports, making it difficult to divert more gas to electricity generation.
According to BPDB data for October 7, six plants or units were offline due to gas shortages. All four units at Ghorashal, with a combined capacity of 1,153MW, were shut.
The Bheramara 410MW, Baghabari 71MW and three Sirajganj units with a combined capacity of 225MW were also offline. Together, these plants have a total capacity of 1,395MW.
Three liquid-fuelled plants, Gopalganj (100MW), Chowmuhani (113MW) and Chapainawabganj (100MW), were also not generating power, with a combined capacity of 313MW.
Six plants or units were unavailable due to maintenance, including Siddhirganj (210MW), Tongi (80MW), Ashuganj East (400MW) and two Barapukuria units (250MW and 274MW), with a combined capacity of 1,339MW.
The BPDB was also not taking power from Haripur (360MW), Meghnaghat (450MW) and Bheramara (20MW) as their contracts had expired. The three plants have a combined capacity of 830MW. The 100MW Shahjibazar gas turbine plant was shut due to a mechanical fault.
Haripur 32MW, Chitttagong 420MW, Shikalbaha Peaking 150MW, Sylhet 20MW and Saidpur 150MW plants were also out of operation.
All units of the coal-fired Barapukuria power plant were shut as well.
The Power Grid Company of Bangladesh (PGCB) said load shedding stood at 2,040MW at 1:00am on October 7 before falling to 859MW at 8:00am. It later rose to 1,161MW at 4pm.
Former Power Cell Director General BD Rahmat Ullah said Bangladesh had failed to follow proper planning while expanding fossil-fuel-based power plants.
“As a result, we have power plants but cannot operate them due to fuel shortages,” he said.
“Since our primary fuel resources are very limited, there is no alternative to shifting to renewable energy.”
He said many countries now generate solar power during the day and store it in batteries for use at night.
“Bangladesh can do the same. The government needs to move forward with proper planning and a clear course of action,” he added.

item.title: Dengue and measles deaths cross 100 in Khulna division
item.description:
The dengue and measles outbreaks in Khulna division have claimed 106 lives and affected 29,109 people since the beginning of the current year, according to the divisional health director’s office.
Of the deaths, 59 were caused by dengue and 47 were among suspected measles cases. The figures were revealed in a report signed by Khulna Divisional Health Director Dr Sheikh Md Mosharraf Hossain on Thursday.
According to the report, 292 dengue patients were admitted to hospitals across the division in the 24 hours to on Thursday morning, while two patients died.
So far this year, 15,621 dengue patients have been admitted to hospitals in the division. Of them, 13,937 have recovered and been discharged, while 392 have been referred elsewhere for better treatment.
Khulna district recorded the highest number of dengue admissions at 5,998, with 23 deaths. Khulna Medical College Hospital admitted 3,057 patients and recorded 27 deaths, including 23 from Khulna.
Bagerhat reported 2,098 admissions and three deaths, Jessore 1,538 and two deaths, Chuadanga 133 and one death, and Jhenaidah 421 and two deaths.
The other districts recorded 571 admissions in Narail, 350 in Magura, 377 in Kushtia, 289 in Meherpur and 464 in Satkhira. Satkhira Medical College Hospital admitted another 325 patients.
Meanwhile, 13,487 suspected measles cases have been reported in the division since March 15. Of them, 443 have been confirmed and 47 suspected measles patients have died.
Khulna district reported 2,427 suspected cases, including 55 confirmed cases and 25 deaths. Kushtia recorded 3,068 suspected cases, 23 confirmed cases and 15 deaths.
Jhenaidah reported 1,121 suspected cases, 17 confirmed cases and five deaths, while Meherpur recorded 784 suspected cases, 10 confirmed cases and one death.
Jessore reported 938 suspected cases, including 58 confirmed cases; Narail 997 suspected and 85 confirmed cases; Bagerhat 989 suspected and 74 confirmed cases; and Satkhira 443 suspected and 34 confirmed cases.
Health authorities said they are continuing to monitor the situation and provide treatment to confirmed and suspected patients.

item.title: Türkiye offers affordable energy solutions to Bangladesh, including FSRUs, LNG
item.description:
Türkiye has expressed a keen interest in bolstering energy ties with Bangladesh by offering efficient and cost-effective power solutions, including cheaper Floating Storage and Regasification Units (FSRUs), Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG), and Heavy Fuel Oil (HFO).
The offer was extended when Turkish Ambassador to Bangladesh Ramis Şen paid a courtesy call on Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Iqbal Hassan Mahmood at his Secretariat office on Thursday.
During the meeting, both sides exchanged views on deepening bilateral relations between Bangladesh and Türkiye, focusing heavily on expanding technical and commercial cooperation in the power and energy sector.
Minister Iqbal Hassan Mahmood emphasized the urgent need for affordable and sustainable energy inputs to help operationalize Bangladesh’s idle power plants and enhance overall national energy security.
Ambassador Ramis Şen was accompanied by Bilal Belyurt, Commercial Counsellor of the Turkish Embassy in Dhaka, alongside a delegation from Turkish energy firm Karpowership, including Jad El Sebaaly, Asli Kilic, and Emma Wahlberg.
The Turkish delegation expressed its readiness to present detailed proposals to ministry officials at the earliest opportunity to support Bangladesh’s energy transition efficiently.
Welcoming the initiative, the minister agreed to hold comprehensive follow-up discussions to examine the technical proposals and identify specific areas of mutual cooperation. Reaffirming Bangladesh's commitment to expanding bilateral energy partnerships, he assured the delegation of continued dialogue.
Ambassador Şen reiterated Türkiye's strong commitment to strengthening multi-sectoral ties with Bangladesh, particularly within the strategic energy landscape.
Md Ziaul Haque, secretary of the Energy and Mineral Resources Division, along with other senior officials of the ministry, was present during the meeting.

item.title: Bangladesh, Lithuania seek to leverage strategic positions to boost connectivity, cooperation
item.description:
Bangladesh and Lithuania on Thursday agreed to leverage their strategic geographic positions in the Baltic region and South and Southeast Asia to promote cooperation, stability and inter-regional connectivity.
They also agreed to celebrate the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations in 2027 in a befitting manner, highlighting the achievements of the bilateral relationship and reaffirming their commitment to further strengthen ties.
The two sides agreed to encourage greater private-sector interaction and exchanges of business delegations to realize the potential for expanded economic cooperation.
The agreements came at the second Foreign Office Consultations (FOC) between Bangladesh and Lithuania held in Dhaka, where both sides placed high priority to recalibrating and expanding bilateral relations, said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Ambassador Dr M Nazrul Islam, Secretary, Bilateral (East & West) of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and Lithuanian Vice-Minister for Foreign Affairs Vidmantas Verbickas led their respective delegations.
Representatives from the Ministry of Commerce, Invest Bangladesh Authority, the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment, and the Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology also participated in the consultations on behalf of Bangladesh.
At the outset of the consultations, the heads of the two delegations signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on the FOC.
The delegations discussed the full range of bilateral relations and stressed the need to further deepen political cooperation. They also proposed reciprocal high-level visits, including by foreign ministers.
Bangladesh highlighted its strengths in key manufacturing sectors, including ready-made garments (RMG), jute and jute products, and pharmaceuticals.
It invited Lithuanian investors to explore the investment-friendly environment in Bangladesh’s Special Economic Zones and urged the early conclusion of an MoU between the apex chambers of commerce of the two countries.
Bangladesh also invited an exploratory mission from the Lithuanian private sector.
Both sides emphasized cooperation in ICT, digital governance, interoperability, e-ID systems, secure data exchange, innovation and business partnerships.
Lithuania expressed its readiness to support e-governance initiatives in Bangladesh.
The delegations also discussed expanding cooperation in information technology, e-registration, e-governance, financial technology (FinTech), GovTech, cloud and data services, cybersecurity, e-transportation, digitization of transport systems, artificial intelligence, innovative technologies, high-tech medical devices, pharmaceuticals and biotechnology.
The Lithuanian vice-minister highlighted Lithuania’s capabilities in these specialized sectors and expressed keen interest in expanding cooperation with Bangladesh, describing it as a rapidly growing digital economy.
The Lithuanian delegation said many Lithuanian digital-sector companies and investors are eager to explore opportunities for investment in Bangladesh and collaborate with Bangladeshi counterparts.
The two sides also discussed cooperation on employment and skilled manpower migration. Bangladesh highlighted its growing pool of skilled workers, including IT professionals, engineers, electricians, plumbers and healthcare workers.
They discussed enhanced cooperation on skilled manpower migration from Bangladesh to Lithuania under the EU’s Talent Partnership program, particularly in ICT, caregiving, construction, hospitality and tourism, agriculture and agro-processing.
Lithuania expressed optimism about the prospects under a government-to-government (G2G) mechanism and through regular legal channels.
The two sides also emphasized the importance of broader people-to-people ties through cooperation in education and sports, exchanges of students, youths, tourists and cultural troupes, and employment opportunities for highly skilled and semi-skilled Bangladeshi workers in Lithuania.
The Lithuanian vice-minister said the number of Bangladeshi students in Lithuania has increased more than fourfold in recent years, with around 1,200 students currently studying at Lithuanian universities.
Bangladesh and Lithuania also agreed to deepen regional and global coordination and reaffirm close coordination and mutual support at international platforms, including the United Nations.
They exchanged views on critical regional and global developments and decided to hold the third round of the Foreign Office Consultations in Vilnius at a mutually convenient time.

item.title: Trump rules out new Iran attack before US midterm elections
item.description:
President Donald Trump on Thursday ruled out attacking Iran before the US midterm elections on 3 November, saying Washington was holding "productive discussions" with Tehran.

Trump's post on his Truth Social platform followed a surge in oil prices on Thursday driven by media reports suggesting potential new US strikes prior to those elections.

"I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect...we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections," he wrote.

"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," he added, without providing additional details.

The Atlantic magazine reported on Wednesday that the White House had asked the Pentagon to develop options to strike Iranian targets that could be used before the midterms. The New York Times published a similar report on Thursday, saying the plans were being developed despite Trump's "ambivalence."

The rise in crude oil prices has also been fueled by persistent tensions in the Strait of Hormuz -- a strategic chokepoint for the global oil trade -- as well as hostilities between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

Polls suggest that US voters are strongly dissatisfied over rising fuel prices, linked to the conflict launched by the United States and Israel against Iran on 28 February.

Brent North Sea crude, the international benchmark, rallied to as high as USD 105.88 a barrel before retreating to USD 104.28.

Iran tells US there is no military solution to Middle East war

Putin vows to help

Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin promised Thursday to "do everything" to help end the Middle East war when he met Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian for talks ahead of a regional summit, Russian media reported.

"We are ready to do everything that is in our power to contribute to the settlement of this situation," Putin said after arriving in Turkmenistan for a summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) that starts Friday in the Caspian Sea resort of Avaza.

He added that Iran had made "real efforts to end the war," according to Russian news agencies.

Russia and Iran have reinforced diplomatic and military links since Russia launched its offensive in Ukraine in February 2022, becoming increasingly reliant on each other.

Trump has repeatedly insisted in recent weeks that the United States has effectively won the Iran war, despite ongoing unrest and a recent security threat that forced the withdrawal of American bombers from a base in England.

But Trump's claims that prices will fall as soon as the Iran war is over have so far fallen on deaf ears with voters.

Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief, Tehran says ready for talks

Approaching election

The midterm elections will shape the final two years of Trump's presidential term as his Republican Party risks losing its current grip on Congress.

Although Trump is not on the ballot, he is holding numerous rallies in an attempt to limit the damage or even turn the political tide.

Trump has warned he faces a possible third impeachment if Democrats retake the House of Representatives, and the White House is preparing for a slew of investigations into corruption and abuse of power.

The US president also on Thursday sought to calm a furor over his comments at a rally earlier this week that Iran could "take out" the cities of Los Angeles and San Diego.

Trump, 80, blamed the "fake and artificial news" for misinterpreting the remarks, which Democrats pounced on.

"In actuality, what I was talking about was that a temporary increase in the price of Gasoline is a small price to pay for Iran not having a Nuclear Weapon and, if you want to see a big price, can you imagine what it would be like if they bombed San Diego and/or Los Angeles?" Trump said on Truth Social.

item.title: Trump administration freezes green cards for Microsoft, IT firms, probes universities
item.description:
• Move follows USD 100,000 fee on fresh H-1B petitions under White House proclamation.

  • Project Firewall has opened about 200 cases and levied millions in penalties.

  • Labor Department will halt new and pending applications involving the named companies

The US suspended Microsoft, major IT outsourcers and software maker Adobe from a key green-card program on Thursday while opening probes into nine top universities, widening a crackdown it says targets fraud and protects American jobs.

Since taking office, US President Donald Trump has pursued a broad effort to reduce the number of foreign-born people in the US and curtail their pathway to residence and citizenship. Thursday's twin actions mark the broadest strike yet against skilled-worker immigration programs — potentially cutting off a common path to permanent residency for foreign tech workers — while putting some of the country's top research universities on notice.

"There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft," Vice President JD Vance said. He said the company laid off 6,000 American workers last year while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B temporary worker visas and nearly 3,000 green cards.

Trump extends push for $100,000 H-1B visas by another year

His comments came hours before Trump honored tech billionaires for their contributions to America, including Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella. Nadella once held an H-1B visa, as did Elon Musk, who was also honored, while three of the other CEOs honored are immigrants.

Nadella thanked Trump for the medal, saying in a post on X he would continue to advance technology and drive American prosperity.

Microsoft is the largest filer of PERM applications, or the permanent labor certification process, according to data from the US labor department. Under PERM, which most employment-based green cards require, employers must show a foreign hire will not hurt US workers' wages or jobs.

The company said in a statement that about 80 per cent of the H-1B applications it filed in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of current employees, not to hire new workers. In July, the company said it would cut 4,800 jobs, or about 2.1 per cent of its global workforce.

Trump administration proposes ending 60-day H-1B visa grace period after job loss

Crackdown Widens

Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the suspension would also cover Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. "We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies," Sonderling said.

He said these companies had since 2009 sought almost three million foreign workers, and had received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications.

Amazon.com was the largest employer of approved H-1B beneficiaries in fiscal 2026, followed by Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Apple and Microsoft, according to US immigration data.

Vance said the suspensions would last "as long as it needs to," and that the administration wanted the companies to change how they hire. He said some companies post ineffective job ads, then point to the lack of applicants to justify hiring lower-paid foreign workers.

Microsoft said in its statement that it pays its H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.

Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, HCL Technologies, Wipro and Capgemini did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Tata Consultancy Services declined to comment.

Nasscom, India's IT industry body, said Indian tech companies in the US had significantly reduced their reliance on H-1B visas, and relatively few of their workers sought green cards through the PERM process.

In September last year, the Labor Department launched an enforcement drive called "Project Firewall" as a White House proclamation imposed a one-time USD 100,000 feeon new H-1B petitions for workers hired from abroad.

H-1B visas for skilled workers: What are they and what changes are coming?

Universities under Scrutiny

Vance also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, would be investigated for what the administration called the misuse of exchange-visitor visas to undercut American wages.

The nine schools also include Brown and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said subpoenas had already been served.

D'Esposito said investigators would examine whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships or visa abuse were compromising federally funded research.

“It could have an enormous economic impact on the whole US economy,” said Sarah Spreitzer, a vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents. International students historically spent USD 40 billion a year while in the US, she said.

The probe deepens the administration's long-running fight with Harvard over foreign students. Last year, the Department of Homeland Security subpoenaed the university over alleged misconduct by international students and its compliance with immigration law. Harvard called that subpoena "unfounded retribution" but said it would comply as far as the law requires.

Rapidly changing visa policies caused a sharp drop in international applications to Columbia University ​and contributed to the university pausing admissions to one of its journalism programs, Reuters reported last week.

Bangladesh doesn’t fully meet minimum standards for eliminating human trafficking
item.description:
Bangladesh has not fully met the minimum standards for the elimination of human trafficking but is making significant efforts to do so, according to the US Department of State’s annual report on human trafficking.

The 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report was published on Thursday. It is available on the US Department of State’s website.

The report said the Bangladesh “government demonstrated overall increasing efforts compared with the previous reporting period; therefore, Bangladesh remained on Tier 2.”. Among Bangladesh’s neighbours, India, Pakistan, Bhutan and Sri Lanka are also in this tier.

Countries that have made significant progress in combating human trafficking and fully met the minimum standards set by relevant US legislation are placed in Tier 1.

Countries that have not fully met the minimum standards but are making significant efforts to do so are placed in Tier 2. A separate Tier 2 Watch List is maintained for certain countries in this category. Countries that have not fully met the minimum standards and are not making significant efforts to do so are placed in Tier 3.

The report said the Bangladesh government’s efforts “efforts included passing the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking and Smuggling of Migrants Ordinance 2026 to strengthen the legal framework to combat trafficking, increasing investigations and prosecutions, updating the human trafficking crime and victim identification guidelines, and piloting a digital NRM to increase timeliness and coordination of referrals to protection services. The government also strengthened protections for migrant workers to reduce vulnerabilities to trafficking.”

However, the Bangladesh government had failed to meet the minimum standards in several key areas. It said fewer human traffickers had been convicted than in the previous reporting period. The government had not taken adequate steps to address internal trafficking crimes, which remained widespread.

The report also said, “The government identified fewer victims, and victim protection and reintegration efforts remained insufficient, particularly for Rohingya refugees and returning Bangladeshi migrant workers.”

“Additionally, the government continued to permit worker-paid recruitment fees that rendered many migrant workers indebted, increasing their vulnerability to trafficking,” the report added.

item.title: Prosecutors in Maradona death trial seek sentences up to 12 years
item.description:
Argentine prosecutors argued on Thursday that the "chaotic" medical team treating football legend Diego Maradona at the time of his death should receive prison sentences up to 12 years.
Seven medical professionals have been on trial since April over Maradona's death on November 25, 2020 while convalescing after surgery for a brain clot.
The star of the 1986 World Cup died of heart failure and acute pulmonary edema -- a condition where fluid accumulates in the lungs -- at a rented home in the Buenos Aires suburb of Tigre two weeks after going under the knife.
The larger-than-life star, who had a history of substance abuse, was 60 at the time of his death.
His medical team, including his chief doctor, psychiatrist, psychologist and nurses, are accused of providing grossly inadequate care in the lead-up to his death. They deny the charges.
In his closing arguments, prosecutor Patricio Ferrai said the defendants' "chaotic organization" left the ailing patient "in a helpless situation, abandoning him to his fate."
He accused them of having "breached their duties, performed actions contrary to the art of healing" and having "omitted all the acts they were required to perform."
The defendants are charged with "dolo eventual" -- a legal term meaning that a person is aware that their actions could cause harm but persisted nonetheless.
The highest prison sentence sought by prosecutors was 12 years, for Maradona's personal physician, Leopoldo Luque.
Other sentences ranging from four to 10 years were sought for other medical staff, which include a psychiatrist, nurse and coordinators.
The health workers have argued that Maradona's death could not have been foreseen and that they did their jobs. Each defendant has also downplayed their own individual responsibility for his care.
The case has revolved around whether the doctors' decision to allow Maradona convalesce in a private home, instead of in a hospital, was negligent.
The prosecution has also pointed to the near-total absence of medical equipment, such as a hospital bed, defibrillator or quickly available ambulance as evidence of what they presented as the defendants' dereliction of duty.
Several medical experts testified that Maradona's carers failed to react to key warning signs -- he was suffering from edema, tachycardia and had difficulty breathing -- in the lead-up to his death.
"Diego Armando Maradona's death clearly did not come out of nowhere: the signs of this fatal outcome began to appear long beforehand," assistant prosecutor Cosme Iribarren summarized on Thursday.
The prosecution again showed the court shock images of the former footballer lying dead in bed, his stomach grotesquely swollen.
Maradona's three daughters, who were present in court on Thursday for the start of the summation, covered their faces to avoid seeing the images.
The summation is expected to last around two weeks and the verdict is expected at a later date.
The first trial over Maradona's death was dramatically annulled last year after two-and-a-half months of hearings, following revelations that one of the judges took part in a clandestine documentary about the case.

item.title: New Ganges waters treaty with guarantee clause emerges as priority for Dhaka
item.description:
Securing its fair share of the transboundary rivers' waters is likely to become a major issue for Bangladesh in the coming days, making effective water diplomacy, international cooperation and constructive engagement with India increasingly important, officials and experts have said.
The urgency is underscored by the Ganges Water Sharing Treaty, signed on December 12, 1996, which is due to expire on the same date this year. The government in Dhaka has been increasingly vocal in recent weeks, communicating a vision that Bangladesh will be seeking a new or revised agreement that safeguards its interests, particularly its share of dry-season flows, with the inclusion of a guarantee clause.
“Water could emerge as one of the major challenges for the entire world, including Bangladesh, in the future,” said Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives Minister Dr Abdul Moyeen Khan on Thursday, stressing the need to integrate proper water management into national development planning.
Bangladesh and India share 54 transboundary rivers, but the Ganges remains the only one covered by a bilateral water-sharing agreement between the two countries.
Water Resources Minister Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee said Bangladesh wants a new or revised Ganges agreement rather than simply renewing the existing treaty, with provisions guaranteeing its required share of water during the dry season.
“Our main priority will be to bring back the guarantee clause that was included in the 1977 agreement,” he said on Thursday.
The 1977 agreement, negotiated by the BNP's founder Ziaur Rahman, included a safeguard stipulating that if the Ganges flow at Farakka fell below the level projected in the treaty to be provided to Bangladesh as its scheduled share during any 10-day period, the release to Bangladesh would not fall below 80% of that share.
An official also referred to Article III of the 1977 agreement, which stipulated that water released to Bangladesh at Farakka should not be reduced below Farakka, except for India's reasonable water uses, not exceeding 200 cusecs, between Farakka and the point where both banks of the Ganges lie within Bangladesh.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir said Bangladesh would seek an outcome that safeguards its national interests and security, including through a possible guarantee clause.
Asked whether the existing treaty would be renewed or replaced with a new agreement, he said, “Whatever is best for Bangladesh’s interest will be done.”
Kobir said Bangladesh’s committee was ready and Dhaka was awaiting a final response from its Indian counterparts.
“Our committee is ready. We are just waiting for the final response from our Indian counterparts. So yes, we are hopeful,” he said.
He also stressed that international law was being taken into consideration in addressing the water-sharing issues.
The Indian government, through its Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal has said that issues concerning the Ganges treaty and other shared rivers would be discussed through the Joint Rivers Commission (JRC).
“On the Ganga Water Treaty, as also other rivers that we share between Bangladesh and India, we have a Joint Rivers Commission. All matters relating to rivers, river-related matters, will be discussed as part of this Joint Rivers Commission,” he said recently, adding that technical-level meetings on the Ganges treaty had continued.
Kobir said sincerity at the political and official levels in both countries was essential to finding an amicable resolution to the long-standing water-sharing issues.
He expressed optimism that the issues could be resolved positively if the leadership of both countries demonstrated a willingness to cooperate.
Anee said water diplomacy should focus on cooperation and mutual benefits rather than competition, stressing the need for sustained dialogue, scientific cooperation, data sharing and inclusive water governance.
“Cooperation should create mutual benefits rather than being framed explicitly as a competition over water,” he said.
He described water as closely linked to Bangladesh’s geography, economy, agriculture, culture, foreign policy and national security.
“We are a delta country shaped by rivers. Yet, we are also a riparian country dependent on water flows originating beyond our borders,” he said.
Anee called for stronger engagement through the JRC and multilateral water governance mechanisms, alongside greater international cooperation and scientific collaboration.
Bangladesh has joined the UN Water Convention, while the Delta Plan 2100 and national river-management initiatives provide a broader framework for addressing long-term water challenges.
“We need cooperation instead of confrontation, evidence instead of assumptions, participation instead of execution, and long-term planning instead of short-term responses,” he said.
“Our goal should not simply be to manage water crises when they occur; our goal should be to build a just, decent, and cooperative water future,” Anee added, calling for greater youth participation in water governance.
Turning to the Teesta, Anee said the river was particularly important for people in northern Bangladesh, where seasonal variations cause water shortages during the dry season and erosion and flooding during the monsoon.
He said the government had placed considerable emphasis on the Teesta project, with feasibility studies and technical assistance underway.
State Minister Kobir also highlighted the importance of water diplomacy on multilateral platforms, stronger international partnerships, technology transfer and scientific cooperation to advance Bangladesh’s interests in transboundary water management.
With the Ganges treaty approaching expiry, Bangladesh faces the task of securing an equitable and sustainable water-sharing arrangement while strengthening cooperation on other shared rivers.
“I think it is very important for Bangladesh and India to renew the Ganges Treaty. But it has to be revised. The very simple reason is that the treaty was done almost three decades ago,” international affairs expert Prof Shahab Enam Khan told UNB recently.
Shahab, who is the executive director of Bangladesh Center for Indo-Pacific Affairs, strongly suggested that this should also come with arrangements such as revitalising the JRC and including a much more transparent and accountable data-sharing system, which will definitely build much more confidence over "hydro-diplomacy" and water management and water sharing, most importantly, between the two countries.
“This is very important that we should also go into the diplomatic negotiations not only from the diplomatic perspective, but also from engineering, science, and definitely economic perspectives,” he said.
Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur, while attending the ninth Indian Ocean Conference in Mauritius, said they would like to see that there is an arrangement and a new treaty, or a revised treaty, ensuring the essential needs of their people.
“These are common rivers, and we have common legacies here, common interests and, as I said, there's no other alternative but to seek a solution that is durable and will win public trust. And this will also be very important to lay the basis for the relationship over the next 25 to 50 years,” he told NDTV on the sidelines of the conference.
The foreign minister said they have done 55 years (of bilateral relations) already. “So, I don't think we should look at five years or ten years. We have to look at the very long term. So, mutual climate resilience as a priority in our foreign policies, our people policy, I should say, will actually be a key driver of the future.”
